Photograph: Darren England/AAP View image in fullscreen The Queensland premier David Crisafulli declared the legislation would give Queensland ‘the strongest bail laws in the country’. Photograph: Darren England/AAP Queensland Queensland concedes law imposing mandatory jail on some offenders as young as 10 breaches human rights State government says ‘breach bail, go to jail’ laws raise risk of overcrowding in jails, while one expert warns they may lead to ‘cruel outcomes’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Ben Smee Queensland state correspondent Thu 27 Aug 2026 07.33 EDT First published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 05.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Queensland government’s latest law and order crackdown – subjecting some children as young as 10 to a mandatory sentence of a year behind bars – could lead to “cruel outcomes”, according to human rights lawyers. In documents tabled with the legislation on Thursday, the government conceded its laws, dubbed “breach bail, go to jail”, would breach human rights and risk further straining the state’s overcrowded jails, youth detention centres and police watch houses. It requires an override of the Queensland Human Rights Act. The legislation applies to a child or adult charged with a “significant offence” while on bail, or failing to appear for a court matter. Europe’s ‘murder capital’ slashed violent crime with a radical program. Will it work in Victoria? Read more For children, a “significant offence” is any of the government’s 47 previously legislated adult crime adult time offences , such as dangerous operation of a vehicle, robbery, and entering a premises and committing an indictable offence. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email For adults, they also additionally include sexual offences against children and coercive control. A person on bail accused of one of the offences would face a much higher bar to be granted bail again. The bill requires that they be remanded in custody unless the court or a police officer is satisfied to a “high degree of confidence” that they would not commit another significant offence. If convicted of the second offence, they would be subjected to a mandatory minimum 12-month sentence, without parole. It could be served concurrently with any other sentence for the additional offence. The law applies even if the person is found not guilty of the first offence. The government concedes that the legislation limits a range of rights including the right to liberty, that persons awaiting trial should not automatically be detained in custody, and the right of children to protection in their best interests. It also concedes that the additional offence will lead to overcrowding in the state’s corrective services facilities and youth detention centre and as a result “will impact the conditions of detention, engaging the right to humane treatment when deprived of liberty”. Under the Queensland Human Rights Act, an override is only permitted where exceptional circumstances, such as a state of emergency, exists. In documents tabled with the bill, the attorney general, Deb Frecklington, said they were “the prevalence of serious repeat offending committed while on bail”. Human rights lawyer Bridget Burton, a senior lecturer at the University of Queensland, said there appeared to be no apparent exceptional circumstances justifying the laws, and they would remove judicial discretion, leading to unreasonable sentences. “Mandatory sentencing prevents judges from considering the circumstances of an offence,” she said. “When circumstances become irrelevant, we can see cruel outcomes for individuals contrary to what the community would expect, particularly when someone who is a victim also commits an offence.” Senior lecturer in criminology and criminal justice at Griffith University William Wood said there was little evidence that a mandatory 12-month sentence would be a strong deterrent for young people. He said the court system could already take into account previous offending when determining whether to grant bail and the law removed that discretion. Wood said the bill would probably affect only the least serious offenders, because a person convicted of a violent offence would already be sentenced to longer than the 12-month term. Queensland already has the highest youth detention rate of any Australian state, and the state already makes “exceptionally heavy use of pre-trial detention,” he said. “Increasing incarceration is not in itself an evidence-based youth crime strategy,” he said. “Once the highest-risk young people are already being detained, expanding detention increasingly captures less serious offenders, with diminishing public-safety returns and growing financial and social costs”. Premier David Crisafulli declared the legislation would give Queensland “the strongest bail laws in the country”. Crisafulli said the state planned to open additional jails, but “faced with the choice of full jails and less [criminal] people in your home, I’ve been upfront about that, and I want to protect Queenslanders”. The legislation also removes the requirement for police to consider diversionary options before charging a child with an offence, and expands an existing exemption to the Human Rights Act in the state’s police watchhouses. Every day, including this one,” he says. He recalls a story of Canadian Lt Leslie Miller, who gathered “a handful of acorns from the shattered European landscape” during the first world war in 1917, carried them home, planted in Ontario and they grew into a majestic forest – with some of them laster repatriated to France and replanted in the same place where they were born.” He says “seeds, values, ideas, trade, people and progress carried back and forth across the Atlantic for centuries.” He continues: “We are not fairweather allies. We do not pursue zero sum deals. Our commitment to the rule of law and our unyielding defence of human dignity, individual freedom and democracy share the same deep roots, the same unwavering dedication. We hold common values for which we have always fought

By Newsfile September 22, 2026 at 8:03 a.m. Miami, Florida–(Newsfile Corp. – September 22, 2026) – IT Monks Agency founder and CEO Alex Osmichenko served as an organizer on the Sponsors Team for WordCamp US 2026 , held Aug. 16-19 at the Phoenix Convention Center in Phoenix, Arizona. WordCamp US 2026 brought the WordPress community to Phoenix for four days of talks, workshops, and contribution To view an enhanced version of this graphic, please visit: https://images.newsfilecorp.com/files/10587/314964_cbf0f192e4acca3f_001full.jpg The four-day WordPress community event included Contributor Day, Showcase Day, and two conference days with more than 50 talks and workshops. Sessions covered topics including WordPress development, block themes, design systems, security, and agency workflows. Artificial intelligence was also a recurring topic at WordCamp US. Alex Osmichenko said discussions centered on how AI can support better quality, faster iterations, and more time for higher-value client work. Those conversations are informing IT Monks Agency’s investments in its team and internal tools. More than 1,100 people registered for WordCamp US 2026, with thousands more watching online. Alex Osmichenko supported returning sponsors, identified and invited prospective partners, and worked to support sponsor participation and encourage returning partnerships. He also proposed consolidating sponsor management for the flagship WordCamp events in Europe, Asia, and the United States into a shared customer relationship management system. The system is intended to give organizing teams access to sponsor contacts, relationship history, and previous outreach across events, helping reduce duplicated work, maintain continuity with past sponsors, and reach new partners more efficiently. The proposal has been adopted and is being implemented ahead of WordCamp Europe 2027, where Alex Osmichenko will again help manage sponsors. “A shared system lets the teams coordinate outreach, avoid duplicated effort, keep continuity with past sponsors, and reach new ones more efficiently,” Alex Osmichenko said. Alex Osmichenko’s WordCamp US role followed his work on the Sponsors Team for WordCamp Europe 2026, held June 4-6 in Kraków, Poland. WordCamp US marked the second flagship WordCamp organizing team he served on this year. “Helping organize both WordCamp Europe and WordCamp US gave me a chance to contribute to the WordPress community from a different side,” Alex Osmichenko said. “You see how much work goes into creating an event where developers, agencies, businesses, and contributors can learn from each other and spend time together. Being part of that work was important to me because WordPress is such a big part of what we do at IT Monks.” The experience also reinforced IT Monks Agency’s focus on contributing to the open-source WordPress community through organizing, sponsorship, WordPress Core participation, and the plugin ecosystem. To learn more about IT Monks Agency, visit https://itmonks.com/ . About IT Monks: IT Monks is a global WordPress agency providing full-cycle digital services across web design, web development, and digital promotion. The agency helps brands create and manage digital experiences through WordPress expertise, strategic solutions, and technical support designed to meet evolving business needs. Photograph: J Miles Cary/Reuters View image in fullscreen Christa Pike in a Knoxville, Tennessee, courtroom in December 2007. Photograph: J Miles Cary/Reuters Tennessee Christa Pike is conscious and speaking after botched execution attempt, lawyers say The prisoner received two doses of pentobarbital last Wednesday as authorities tried to put her to death Guardian staff and agencies Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.21 EDT First published on Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.05 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Christa Pike, a Tennessee prisoner who survived the state’s attempt to execute her, is awake and speaking as she receives treatment at a hospital, her attorneys said on Tuesday. Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital as Tennessee officials attempted to put her to death in a case that shocked many in America and created headlines around the world. She was set to be the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. “Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking and continues to receive critical medical care. Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed. Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery,” attorneys for Pike said in a statement. Her attorneys said they are grateful for the first responders and the medical team at the hospital “who treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her”. They added Pike was “still handcuffed and ‌shackled to the bed”. The statement was the first indication that Pike has improved since an ambulance carried her away from a Nashville prison last Wednesday. Witnesses to the attempt to execute Pike described how they they heard she was choking and struggling for an hour after receiving the first injection. She was then hospitalized after a second dose failed to kill her. In hospital she was put on a ventilator and had been in critical condition. The disastrous attempt sparked widespread condemnation across the political spectrum and among advocates for banning the death penalty. Tennessee’s prison chief, Frank Strada, also resigned in the aftermath as Pike’s experience was the fifth botched execution under his leadership across two states since 2022. Pike was given a death for the torture and killing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow student at the Knoxville Job Corps, in 1995. Pike was 18 at the time. Her then boyfriend and co-defendant, Tadaryl Shipp, was 17 and was ineligible for the death penalty. He received a sentence of life imprisonment. In the wake of the botched execution attempt Helen Prejean, a Catholic nun who is perhaps the best-known advocate for abolition of the death penalty in America, told the Guardian : “This is the essence of cruelty. Take a conscious, imaginative human being, give her a date for her death, have her anticipate it over and over again, and then take her out and try and kill her. “She was rendered defenceless as they deliberately attempted to kill her – what greater mental torture for a human being is there?” The Associated Press contributed to this report Explore more on these topics Tennessee Capital punishment US crime US justice system news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

The Queen was shown boarding a Gripen on 8 October at an airfield in Surat Thani province, southern Thailand, while King Maha Vajiralongkorn watched from the ground. The Royal Household has said she is an experienced pilot, having logged about 1,188 hours across several types of aircraft since she began flying in 2010. She also co-piloted aircraft carrying the King on official visits to other countries, the Royal Household said. https://www.dailypress.com/2026/09/30/ar.text: “The Other Mozart,” a play about Nannerl Mozart, Amadeus’ genius sister, will be performed in the Glenn Close Theatre on Saturday. (Charlotte Dobre) By John Shulson | Correspondent PUBLISHED: September 30, 2026 at 9:30 AM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... October is going to be a month filled with performing arts activities, starting with William & Mary’s “Presents!” series. On Saturday, “The Other Mozart” plays in the university’s Glenn Close Theatre at 7:30 p.m. This is an award-winning play created by Sylvia Milo that deals with Nannerl Mozart, the brilliant sister of Amadeus. Nannerl was considered a prodigy, keyboard virtuoso and composer who performed throughout Europe with her brother until their father, aware of his daughter’s very popular reception, decided it was not appropriate for a female to be touring and should stay at home. Thus, her name and acclaim were lost to history until 2013, when the play debuted and has been shown worldwide. The Nannerl character, played interchangeably by Milo and Daniela Galli, owns the stage in an 18-foot gown designed by the National Theater of Poland. Joshua Rose, an assistant theater professor at W&M, previously toured with the show as its lighting designer and technical consultant. Then at 2 p.m. Sunday in the Concert Hall, “Presents!” offers the world premiere of “The Triangle Suite,” written by Williamsburg composer Fred Strong and commissioned by the Office of the Arts at the university. The five-movement piano work weaves together elements and artistry of the Historic Triangle. Performing will be internationally-acclaimed and award-winning Brazilian American Daniel Inamorato, a faculty pianist at W&M. The fare will also feature piano works by W&M composer Eric Lyttle and other Virginia composers, all in celebration of America’s 250th anniversary. For tickets to these two events, visit wm.universitytickets.com . The second Members Co-Op Show at the Williamsburg Contemporary Art Center opened Sept. 16 and runs through Oct. 30. The participating artists are, from left, Marharyta Pendiur, Jessica Swan, Ted Lyman, Lisa Adele Cumming, Penny Trexel, Bud Longo, Laurie Jost, Dennis Jagoda and Patricia Spayd. (Trudi Arnold is not pictured). Art center hours are Wednesday through Saturday from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. and Sunday from 1-4 p.m. (Michael D. Jones) Virginia Choral Society Established in 1931, the Virginia Choral Society is one of the oldest continuously performing vocal ensembles in the state. It opens its new season at 4 p.m. Oct. 11 in King of Glory Lutheran Church. “United We Sing” offers a program of choral works representing South Africa, Norway, Mexico and China (among others), most, if not all sung in native languages. For tickets, visit vachoralsociety.org or purchase at the door. Williamsburg Symphony Orchestra The Williamsburg Symphony Orchestra’s season continues Oct. 13 with “Sonic Portraits” in the Williamsburg Community Chapel. The fare leads off with Carlos Simon’s “The Block,” inspired by Romare Bearden’s African American series of painting that essentially explored the vivid and cultural life in Harlem, as found in neighborhood buildings. World-acclaimed violinist Rachel Barton Pine takes to the stage in the Brahms Violin Concerto, his only such concerto. Expect passion, richness of sound and elegance of delivery, most notably in the exquisite second movement, totally enhanced by Pine, who is considered one of the finest interpreters of classical masterworks in the world. The program closes with Paul Hindemith’s “Mathis der Maler Symphony.” Hindemith was openly critical of the Nazis, so after the symphony’s successful debut with the Berlin Philharmonic in 1934, it was banned. He ultimately left Germany, went to Switzerland and to the United States in 1940. It’s a powerful and exciting work. The performance starts at 7:30 p.m., with a preconcert talk at 6:30 p.m. For tickets, visit williamsburgsymphony.org . Williamsburg Choral Guild The Williamsburg Choral Guild’s current season opens Oct. 17 in the Williamsburg Presbyterian Church with the beautiful Maurice Duruflé “Requiem.” Michelle Kwok, artistic director of the guild and visiting assistant teaching professor at W&M, conducts. It is based on Gregorian chants but with inspiration derived from Debussy and Fauré. It is best described in Duruflé’s own words: “This Requiem is not an ethereal work which sings of detachment from earthly worries. It reflects, in the immutable form of the Christian prayer, the agony of man faced with the mystery of his ultimate end. It is often dramatic, or filled with resignation, or hope or terror, just as the words of the Scripture themselves, which are used in the liturgy. It tends to translate human feelings before their terrifying, unexplainable or consoling destiny.” The show starts at 7:30 p.m., with a pre-concert talk at 7 p.m. For tickets, visit williamsburgchoralguild.org . Bruce Hornsby Williamsburg’s own (along with his Noise Makers) winds down his “ Indigo Park” album tour in the Ferguson Center for the Arts in Newport News at 7:30 p.m. Oct. 17, courtesy of the Virginia Arts Festival. The album was released this past April and includes songs that “oscillate between extremes — light and dark, memory and fantasy, calm and rage and doubt and certainty.” Throughout his acclaimed career, Hornsby has pushed the creative envelope in working well beyond pop, adapting styles and techniques of forward-thinking, Webern-associated composers, blending such disparate aspects as jazz, minimalism and classical structures into his own successful sound. For tickets, visit vafest.org . Open Door Concert Series The diverse and quite entertaining Open Door Series opens its season at 4 p.m. Oct. 18 in the Williamsburg Presbyterian Church with Tuba Skinny. Tuba Skinny and its New Orleans street music blends traditional jazz, ragtime, spirituals, country blues and New Orleans R&B into its now internationally-celebrated sound. Free and fun. Recap Miró Quartet’s Hennage performance on Sept. 15 was splendid, as are all of the offerings provided by the Chamber Music Society. Haydn’s D Major Quartet was, as expected, delightful and exciting; Shaw’s “Entr’acte” complex and interesting; Webern’s “Langsamer Satz” extraordinarily beautiful and sensitive; and Dvořák’s “American” a listening pleasure. The quartet’s performances were, not surprisingly, terrific. An added attraction to the visit was the program presented to students at Matthew Whaley Elementary School the morning of the concert as part of the society’s educational outreach initiative. It was a chance to see and hear the musicians in a very informal environment. Dressed in jeans and with calculated and curated silliness, the quartet held the attention of the kids as each member talked about themselves, their instruments and things to listen for in the segments being played, from serious to toe-tapping fiddle playing. The Williamsburg Symphony Orchestra’s opening “Fire and Fantasy” program on Sept. 22 was an equally smashing success. Musical director Michael Butterman’s comments on Anna Clyne’s “Pivot” provided clarity out of potential confusion. And he provided brief projection screen narratives to explain the shifting emotions and visual happenings in the ballet score to “Petrushka,” which brought focus into the colorful score. Performances were over-the-top wonderful, as was the featured playing of Evren Ozel in the Rach 2 Piano Concerto with its lush, sumptuous, exciting lines, which Ozel delivered in aces, matched by the WSO. Have information about the arts in the Historic Triangle? Contact John Shulson at johnshulson@gmail.com. https://enrsi.stvr.sk/articles/Culture/4.text: Ľubomír Feldek Turns 90, Celebrating a Lifetime of Slovak Literature Books for children are also part of the rich and diverse body of work of prominent Slovak poet and playwright Ľubomír Feldek, who turns 90 today, 9 October. To mark the occasion, the Slovak National Theatre is putting on a special programme featuring poetry readings, a theatrical performance, recollections of past collaborations, and live music. The event takes place Saturday, 10 October, in Bratislava. Slovak Literature Takes the Spotlight at the Frankfurt Book Fair From 7 to 11 October, the Frankfurt Book Fair brings together more than 7,500 exhibitors from over 100 countries. Slovakia is represented by Miroslava Kuľková, who will present her debut short-story collection, Hotel Balkán. Bratislava-based authors Mária Modrovich and Tomáš Hučko will take part in a Czech-Slovak discussion as part of the Czech Republic’s Guest of Honour programme. The Slovak Literary Centre’s stand will also welcome members of the Slovak PEN Centre: Mária Bátorová, Milan Richter, and Vladimír Skalský. Sláva Daubnerová’s Melancholia Returns to the Stockholm Stage On 9, 12, 14, 17 and 19 October, audiences in Stockholm can see Melancholia, the acclaimed film by Lars von Trier, reimagined for the stage by Slovak director Sláva Daubnerová. The Swedish Royal Opera commissioned Daubnerová to bring this experimental production to the stage in 2023. The production returned to the Royal Opera’s programme in October 2026, once again attracting attention. Another Slovak connection is internationally acclaimed stage designer Boris Kudlička, who contributed to the opera production. Writing in the journal kØd in 2016, theatre critic Katarína Cvečková described Daubnerová’s distinctive approach: “Where Daubnerová differs from her Slovak theatre contemporaries is her unique theatrical language, which she employs mainly in creation of her own plays. She is significant for taking up unusual topics, employment of documentary theatre elements, blending of genres and overlapping of multiple artistic styles.” A Classic by Juraj Jakubisko Featured at the Lumière Festival in Lyon The Lumière Festival celebrates major works from cinema history and highlights the importance of preserving film heritage. The Treasures and Curiosities section presents some of the finest restored films of the 20th century, including lesser-known works and films that have long remained hidden in the archives. This year, Slovakia is represented in the section, which features nearly 40 films, by Juraj Jakubisko’s Birds, Orphans and Fools (1969). The film has also been selected for the Re>Birth programme at the International Classic Film Market (MIFC), which takes place during the festival from 13 to 16 October. An Evening of Experimental Music at Bratislava’s Old Lyceum The Chamber Concerts and Dialogues at the Old Lyceum series continues on Tuesday, 13 October, with an evening dedicated to composer Martin Štefánik and his Kinetic Composition project. The event takes place in the historic Old Lyceum hall in Bratislava. Here’s programme manager Barbara Sigmundová with an invitation to the event.
